Why Do We Test Fitness?

Fitness testing is a core tool in any serious training programme. Rather than guessing whether a performer is getting fitter, a coach can use objective data to make decisions that are evidence-based and precise. When used properly, test results drive every stage of the coaching cycle — from identifying what needs work, to setting goals, to measuring whether training is actually producing results. Understanding why fitness testing matters, and how to use results wisely, is essential knowledge for anyone working in sport and coaching.

Establishing a Baseline

Before any training programme begins, a coach must know where the performer currently stands. This starting-point measurement is called a baseline. Without a baseline, it is impossible to measure progress — a performer might feel fitter after six weeks of training, but only test scores recorded at the start can prove it. The baseline also allows the coach to identify which components of fitness are already at an acceptable level and which urgently need development. For example, a netball player might score well on agility but poorly on cardiovascular endurance; the baseline reveals this immediately.

Once a baseline is recorded, the same tests are repeated at regular intervals throughout the programme. This is called monitoring progress. Comparing repeated test scores against the baseline tells the coach and performer whether training is producing the desired adaptations. If scores stagnate or decline, it signals that the programme needs adjusting — perhaps by increasing intensity, changing training methods or addressing recovery.

Key Fact

The six reasons for fitness testing are: to carry out comparisons against normative data, to identify a performer's strengths and weaknesses, to provide a baseline for future comparisons, to provide important information for the coach, to provide information that assists in team selection, and to set goals or targets.

Identifying Strengths and Weaknesses

Fitness testing allows a coach to build a detailed profile of a performer across all relevant components. For instance, a footballer might be tested on speed (30m sprint), agility (Illinois agility run), cardiovascular endurance (multistage fitness test), and muscular strength (hand grip or rep max). The results show which components are a strength and which are a weakness that limits performance. This targeting prevents training from becoming unfocused. A coach will not waste a sprinter's limited training time on flexibility work if speed is the weakness that most affects their event. Testing turns vague impressions into specific, actionable priorities.

Setting Goals with SMART Targets

Without test data, goal-setting tends to be vague — "get fitter" or "run faster" give a performer no clear direction. Test results make it possible to set SMART targets: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-phased. For example, if a basketball player scores 9 shuttles on the multistage fitness test, a SMART short-term target might be "reach level 10 within eight weeks." This is specific (multistage test level 10), measurable (an objective number), achievable and realistic (one level above current), and time-phased (eight weeks). SMART goals give the performer something concrete to aim at, which research consistently links to better exercise adherence and effort in training.

Test results also help a coach design and adapt the training programme itself. If a swimmer's repeat sprint data shows that their lactate threshold is lower than expected, the coach can introduce more aerobic interval work at the appropriate training zone. As fitness improves, re-testing allows the programme to be updated — loads, rest periods or methods can be adjusted to match the performer's current level, ensuring continued progression rather than a plateau.

Key Fact

SMART targets turn raw test scores into meaningful goals. A baseline test result is the starting point; the SMART target describes the desired test result by a specific future date. The coach then designs the training programme to close the gap between the two.

Motivating the Performer

Seeing measurable improvement is one of the most powerful motivators in sport. When a performer's re-test results show that their sit-up score has increased from 32 to 45 in six weeks, the data provides concrete evidence that their hard work is paying off. This boosts confidence and sustains engagement with the programme. Conversely, when results plateau, the data can motivate a performer to refocus and try harder. Many coaches share test results openly with their athletes precisely for this motivational effect, using progress charts to make improvements visible.

Team Selection and Normative Data

Fitness test results provide information that assists with team selection. A coach selecting players for a squad can use objective data to compare performers against each other rather than relying on subjective impressions from matches. Test scores can also be compared against normative data — published tables of average scores for a test, broken down by age and gender. Normative data shows whether a performer's result is poor, average, above average or excellent compared with the wider population or with elite performers in their sport. For example, a 16-year-old male who scores a vertical jump of 50 cm can compare this against published normative tables to see that this sits in the "above average" category.

Validity and Reliability of Testing

Validity refers to whether a test genuinely measures what it is supposed to measure. A test is valid if the component it measures directly reflects what is required in the performer's sport. For example, the multistage fitness test has high validity for sports that require sustained cardiovascular endurance, such as distance running or football. However, it would have low validity if used to assess muscular strength — it simply does not measure that component.

Reliability refers to the consistency of a test — if the same performer takes the same test under the same conditions on two occasions, a reliable test will produce very similar scores. Reliability is affected by factors such as the time of day the test is taken, the performer's hydration and fatigue levels, the equipment used, and whether the tester follows a standardised protocol. If a test is not reliable, then comparing results across time or between performers becomes meaningless. A coach who discovers their testing procedure is inconsistent cannot trust the data, and any conclusions drawn — about progress, goal-setting or selection — will be flawed.

Normative data is only useful if the test that produced your result was administered in exactly the same way as the test that produced the normative data. If a performer completes the sit-and-reach flexibility test on a cold day without warming up, but the normative table was built from scores taken after a 10-minute warm-up, the comparison is invalid. This is why standardising test protocols — same time of day, same warm-up, same equipment, same instructions — is essential. Validity matters here too: a poorly chosen test that does not reflect the relevant component will produce a score that cannot be meaningfully placed against normative data for that component. Coaches must always use a recognised, standardised protocol to ensure both validity and reliability before trusting any comparison.

A coach typically uses a battery of tests — several different tests covering multiple components — at the start of a training block to build a full fitness profile. The results are recorded, compared against normative data, and used to set SMART targets for each component. As the programme progresses, the same tests are repeated (often every four to six weeks) and the results are compared to the baseline. The coach can then make informed decisions: increase load if progress is slower than expected, introduce new training methods if one component is not responding, or ease volume if recovery data suggests fatigue is accumulating. This cycle of test, analyse, adapt and re-test is the backbone of evidence-based coaching.
